entities.text: High Court Of Judicature At Allahabad
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The petitioner was employed as Constable (Civil Police) with U.P. Police.
On 17.5.2008, the petitioner was given the responsibility to produce prisoners before the concerned Session Courts.

The petitioner was handed over custody of one Mithilesh, an under - trial prisoner, charged as an accused in Session Trial No. 83, 5A / 2003 and Case Crime No. 197 of 2001 registered under Sections 302 / 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
The aforesaid accused was in District Jail, Kanpur Nagar and was handed over to the petitioner to be produced in the court of Additional Sessions Judge, Court No. 12, District Kanpur Nagar.

entities.text: Additional Sessions Judge, Court No. 12, District Kanpur Nagar
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The petitioner did not return with the accused and did not hand over the custody of the prisoner in the lock up and the prisoner had escaped.

sentences.text: On medical examination, it was found that the petitioner had consumed liquor.

A perusal of the records shows that the prisoner was an accused in six different cases, two of which were registered under Sections 302 and 307 IPC and two cases were registered under the N.D.P.S. Act while two other cases were registered under Sections 25 / 27 Arms Act.
The allegation against the petitioner was that he had purposely and knowingly allowed the prisoner to escape.

The disciplinary authority concluded that as the petitioner had colluded with the prisoner who was a notorious criminal and allowed him to escape, therefore, no one would come forward to give evidence against the petitioner in the departmental proceedings and the petitioner would be discharged in the departmental proceedings because of lack of evidence.
The disciplinary authority also noted that there was sufficient evidence against the petitioner to award major punishment.

On the aforesaid conclusion, the disciplinary authority recorded its satisfaction that it would not be reasonably practicable to hold a departmental inquiry before proceeding to award major punishment to the petitioner.

Consequently, on the basis of evidence on record and in exercise of his powers under Section 8(2)(b) of the Uttar Pradesh Police Officers of Subordinate Ranks (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1991 (hereinafter referred to as,
'Rules, 1991'), the Senior Superintendent of Police, Kanpur Nagar, i.e., the disciplinary authority,
vide order dated 18.5.2008 dismissed the petitioner from service.

entities.text: Uttar Pradesh Police Officers of Subordinate Ranks (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1991
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: While awarding major punishment to the petitioner, the disciplinary authority also took note of the conduct of the petitioner as Constable.

It has been noted in the order that the petitioner, after consuming liquor,
misbehaved with the public and committed acts of indiscipline and indulged in activities which lowered the reputation of the police force.

The records also reveal that the petitioner had previously also been given punishments for having committed acts of indiscipline and misconduct and further,
Case Crime No. 143 / 1992 under Sections 302 / 376 IPC had also been registered against the petitioner.
The order dated 18.5.2008 was challenged by the petitioner in appeal which was dismissed by the Inspector General of Police, Kanpur Nagar vide his order dated 10.6.2019.
The orders dated 18.5.2008 and 10.6.2019 have been challenged in the present petition.

It was argued by the counsel for the petitioner that the order dated 18.5.2008 dismissing the petitioner from service has been passed without giving any opportunity of hearing to the petitioner and is, therefore, in violation of the principles of natural justice and Rule 8 of the Rules, 1991.
It was argued that for the aforesaid reason, the order is also violative of Articles 14 and 311(2) of the Constitution of India.

It was further argued that there was no material before the Senior Superintendent of Police, i.e., the disciplinary authority to dispense with the inquiry stipulated in Rule 8 of the Rules, 1991 on the ground that it was not reasonably practicable to hold an inquiry against the petitioner and the power under Section 8(2)(b) of the Rules, 1991 has been mechanically exercised by the disciplinary authority.
It was further argued that no reasons have been given in the impugned order dated 18.05.2008 for dispensing with the inquiry.
It was argued that in his order dated 10.6.2019, the Inspector General of Police, Kanpur Region, Kanpur has not considered the aforesaid aspects.
It was argued that for the aforesaid reasons, the orders dated 18.5.2008 and 10.6.2019 are contrary to law and liable to be quashed.
Rebutting the arguments of the counsel for the petitioner, the Standing Counsel representing the respondents has supported the orders dated 18.5.2008 and 10.6.2019 and the reasons given in the same.

sentences.text: In its order dated 18.5.2008, the disciplinary authority has noticed the different cases that were registered against the accused Mithilesh who was to be produced in the Session Court on 17.05.2008 by the petitioner.
On the basis of the cases registered against the prisoner, the disciplinary authority concluded that Mithilesh was a notorious criminal.
The petitioner did not immediately report to his superiors that Mithilesh had escaped.
The petitioner was found missing and on search, he was found on the sixth floor of the court building.
The aforesaid facts were sufficient for the disciplinary authority to infer that the petitioner had colluded with Mithilesh and allowed him to escape from custody.

In the circumstances, no perversity has been committed by the disciplinary authority to hold that due to fear of Mithilesh, no witness would have appeared against the petitioner and the petitioner would have been discharged in the departmental proceedings because of lack of evidence.
The disciplinary authority also noticed that the petitioner himself was an accused under Sections 302/376 IPC and had also previously been punished for acts of indiscipline.

On the aforesaid facts, I find no illegality in the order passed by the disciplinary authority holding that it was not reasonably practicable to hold a disciplinary inquiry and passing order of major punishment exercising its powers under Section 8(2)(b) of the Rules, 1991.

In its impugned order dated 18.5.2008, the disciplinary authority has recorded its satisfaction that the conduct of the petitioner had not only lowered the reputation of the police force but retaining the petitioner in service would have an adverse impact on the discipline and sincerity of the police force and further, serious adverse consequences may ensue regarding protection of ammunition and state property, therefore, it was not desirable to retain the petitioner in service.

A perusal of the facts stated above also shows that prompt action was required in the matter and the impugned order has been passed by the disciplinary authority after considering the material available on record and also after considering the evidence in support of the punishment imposed on the petitioner.
The disciplinary authority has also considered the previous conduct of the petitioner as Constable.
The disciplinary authority had also noticed that instead of reporting to his superiors on 17.5.2008, the petitioner was found consuming liquor after allowing the prisoner to escape.
There was sufficient material to award major punishment including the medical report which showed that the petitioner was under the influence of liquor.

In Satyavir Singh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors. 1985 (4) SCC 252, the Supreme Court held that while holding that it was not reasonably practicable to hold an inquiry under Article 311(2) Proviso - II (b) which is pari materia to Rule 8(2)(b) of the Rules, 1991, 'the court must put itself in the place of the disciplinary authority and consider what in the then prevailing situation a reasonable man acting in a reasonable manner would have done.

entities.text: Satyavir Singh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors. 1985 (4) SCC 252
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It will judge the matter in the light of the then prevailing situation and not as if the disciplinary authority was deciding the question whether the inquiry should be dispensed with or not in the cool and detached atmosphere of a court room,
removed in time from the situation in question.
Where two views are possible, the court will decline to interfere.'

Further, in Paragraph - 21 of the aforesaid report the Supreme Court observed as follows:-
"21.

The point which was next urged in support of the contention that the impugned orders were passed mala fide was that even though co-workers may not have been available as witnesses, there were policemen and police officers posted inside and Mahesh Kumar vs State Of U.P. And 2 Others on 15 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88428458/
3 outside the building and they were available to give evidence and that superior officers were also available to give evidence.

entities.text: Mahesh Kumar vs State Of U.P. And 2 Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The crucial and material evidence against the appellants would be that of their co- workers for these co-workers were directly concerned in and were eyewitnesses to the various incidents.

Where the disciplinary authority feels that crucial and material evidence will not be available in an inquiry because the witnesses who could give such evidence are intimidated and would not come forward and the only evidence which would be available, namely, in this case, of policemen, police officers and senior officers, would only be peripheral and cannot relate to all the charges and that, therefore, leading only such evidence may be assailed in a court of law as being a mere farce of an inquiry and a deliberate attempt to keep back material witnesses, the disciplinary authority would be justified in coming to the conclusion that an inquiry is not reasonably practicable."

In light of the aforesaid observations of the Supreme Court in Satyavir Singh (supra), I do not find any illegality in the orders dated 18.5.2008 and 10.6.2019 calling for interference by this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
The petition lacks merit and is, hereby, dismissed.
